🇲🇽🗳️ <u>Morena's mass base dwarfs the PAN in Mexico City</u>

The rolls tell the story of Mexico's realignment. Heading into 2027, Morena counts more than 1.1 million members in Mexico City alone, while the right-wing PAN crawled from about 18,000 to just 38,314 affiliates, according to INE-certified party registries. Nationally, 43% of Mexicans identify with Morena, per the latest Enkoll poll — as the PRI and Movimiento Ciudadano keep shrinking.

🚨🇲🇽 <u>Guerrero sweep: 71 armed "police" detained, 284 guns seized</u>

In a coordinated operation across Tlapa, Chilapa and Atlixtac, Guerrero's Operativo Enjambre detained 71 armed men working as "police" and seized 284 firearms. The 66 who proved they were accredited officers were released; five remain under investigation — among them Tlapa's transport director and three Chilapa officers accused of unlawful detention and abuse of authority. The state is auditing exactly who carries a badge and a gun in the Montaña.

🔥🇲🇽 <u>Purépecha to the government: rights mean land, not just recognition</u>

Purépecha communities in Michoacán are pushing back on the government's own Indigenous rights bill — not to reject rights, but to demand more. The Council of Indigenous Communities (CSIM) refuses to let the INPI speak for them and calls the draft "a setback" because it fails to guarantee territory, direct budgets, and community control over security, justice and water, including Lake Zirahuén. Self-determination, they insist, has to include the land.

🇲🇽📚 <u>Governments have always wanted the rural teacher colleges gone</u>

The normales rurales — where "the children of peasants, workers and low-income families study" — are still in the crosshairs. Specialist Hallier Morales tells La Jornada that federal and state governments "have always sought to disappear these schools, because they are spaces of resistance and organization, not only of students but of communities." Ayotzinapa is the most famous of them; eleven years after the 43, the pressure on rural normalismo has never let up.

🇲🇽⚖️ <u>Mexico's elected Supreme Court turns one</u>

One year ago Mexico did what no country had dared: it chose its Supreme Court justices by popular vote. Today the renewed judiciary marks its first anniversary, with President Sheinbaum in attendance and Chief Justice Hugo Aguilar Ortiz — the first Indigenous person to lead the Court — presenting the balance. The 2024 reform closed the door on a judicial caste that for decades shielded the powerful; the bench elected on Sept. 1 now answers to the voters who put it there.

🔥🇲🇽 <u>Madrid, the oligarchy's "new Miami"</u>

While Sheinbaum governs for the poor, Mexico's old ruling class has found its refuge in Spain. Ex-presidents Calderón, Peña Nieto and Salinas all enjoy golden retirements in Madrid; ex-teachers' union boss Elba Esther Gordillo shops the Salamanca district out of the five-star Wellington; and Mexicans have poured over €700 million into Spanish real estate since 2020, La Jornada reports — Salamanca is now nicknamed "the new Polanco."

🇲🇽⚡ <u>MEXICO'S AI BOOM HITS THE GRID</u>

Mexico's data-center capacity nearly tripled in two years — from 115 MW in early 2024 to 279 MW today, 72% of it in Querétaro, with the industry targeting 1.5 GW by 2030. The catch isn't demand, it's the grid: under the old neoliberal model only 11% of the approved transmission budget was ever spent, per IMCO — which makes CFE's expansion the real nearshoring battleground. (El Economista)

🇲🇽🏗️ <u>76 BILLION PESOS FOR MEXICO'S FORGOTTEN EAST</u>

The Plan Integral for the eastern State of Mexico just hit 40% completion: 121 projects worth 75.8 billion pesos in water, health, housing and transit for the 10 million people of Neza, Chalco, Ecatepec, Chimalhuacán and Valle de Chalco — the densest, most neglected corner of the country. This month IMSS breaks ground on four new childcare centers, and Governor Delfina Gómez reports homicides in the zone already down 33%.

🇲🇽💧 <u>MEXICO RECLAIMS 5 BILLION m³ OF WATER FROM PRIVATE HANDS</u>

After December's reform stripped water of its status as a tradable commodity and restored it as a human right, Mexico has recovered more than 5 billion cubic meters from private concessions — enough to supply 90 million people for a year. Cities like Mexicali and Tijuana now hold their water rights directly, instead of buying back what neoliberalism privatized out from under them.

🇲🇽📉 <u>HOMICIDES DOWN 51% IN UNDER TWO YEARS</u>

Mexico's daily homicide rate has fallen 51% since Sheinbaum took office — from 86.9 killings a day in September 2024 to 42.5 in July 2026, 44 fewer bodies every single day, per the national security secretariat (SESNSP). July marked the lowest monthly average in 11 years.
